identifier: W. F. Meggers and C. G. Peters, "Measurements on the index of refraction of air for wave lengths from 2218 A to 9000 A", Bulletin of the Bureau of Standards 14, 697-740 (1918); signed Washington, March 13, 1918. The value entered is the 5900 A row of Table 5 (p. 731), column (n-1)10^7.
grade_rule: E3, grade_tag peer_reviewed. Another laboratory's measurement, capped at E3 by 10.3 rule 1 however carefully it was made.
license_note: United States government work, public domain. Numeric table values and stated measurement conditions only. No text or figure is reproduced.
method_as_stated: Fabry and Perot interferometer inside a chamber whose air temperature and pressure were regulated. Circular fringe sections were photographed with a grating or rock-salt prism spectrograph, first with the space between the plates evacuated and then with dry air at measured temperature and pressure, giving the ratio of a wavelength in vacuum to the same wavelength in air directly. Observations at roughly 40 A intervals from 2200 A to 9000 A. Complete sets were made on DRY air at atmospheric pressure at 0, 15 and 30 degC: 277 measurements at 0 degC, 513 at 15 degC, 375 at 30 degC, 1165 in all. The measurements were grouped into 34 points at 200 A intervals and reduced by least squares to a three-constant Cauchy formula at each temperature; the paper gives the probable error of a single (n-1)10^7 as 3.8 at 0 degC, 3.1 at 15 degC and 2.9 at 30 degC.
how_the_tabulated_value_was_produced: TABLE 5 IS COMPUTED FROM THE PAPER'S OWN 15 degC DISPERSION EQUATION, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO: 'The dispersion equation representing our observations on the indices of refraction of air at 15 C and 760 mm was used to construct a new table of corrections.' As with Tilton and Taylor, this is the authors' own least-squares reduction of their own measurements, published in the primary paper, which is not rule 5's excluded case.
why_this_and_not_the_alternatives: The modern primaries are all paywalled and were recorded as inaccessible rather than worked around: Ciddor, Appl. Opt. 35, 1566 (1996) at Optica; Birch and Downs, Metrologia 30, 155 (1993) and 31, 315 (1994); Peck and Reeder, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 62, 958 (1972). A full-text copy of Ciddor 1996 is served from a personal website and was deliberately NOT fetched -- retrieving it would be working around a paywall, which this agent does not do. NIST's Engineering Metrology Toolbox documentation (Stone and Zimmerman, 2001, emtoolbox.nist.gov) reproduces the Ciddor and modified-Edlen equations and is a calculator's documentation reproducing published equations, which rule 5 keeps out as a source for those equations. What was left was this paper, which is a primary measurement, is in the public domain, and prints the quantity on a 50 A grid.
note: READ FROM THE PRINTED TABLE, WHICH GIVES REFRACTIVITY AND NOT INDEX. Table 5's second column is (n-1)10^7; at 5900 A it reads 2764.66, so n = 1.000276466. That is a rewriting of the printed number in the form the registry's unit `1` takes, not a derivation -- no other quantity enters and nothing is fitted or interpolated. Cross-checked against the modern value: Ciddor's equation for dry air at 15 degC and 101.325 kPa near 590 nm gives 1.0002765, agreeing with this 1918 measurement to the eighth decimal, which is the strongest available evidence that the scanned digits were read correctly.
not_entered: The rest of Table 5 -- (n-1)10^7 on a 50 A grid from 2000 A to 10000 A, together with the vacuum correction to wavelength and to frequency at each -- and the three Cauchy dispersion equations at 0, 15 and 30 degC. The grid points include 6050 A, so if the emission path's nominal 605 nm is settled as the wavelength A6 works at, air can be filed at exactly that wavelength from this same table with no interpolation. The Cauchy coefficients were NOT transcribed: the OCR of this scan garbles them and they were not confirmed against the page image, because nothing needed them.
caveat: DRY AIR, AND THE BENCH'S AIR IS NOT DRY. The measurement is on dry air at 760 mm; laboratory air carries water vapour, which lowers the index by of order 1e-6 per 10 per cent relative humidity at visible wavelengths. That is four orders of magnitude below anything an axial range is quoted to, but it is a condition the entry does not cover and the validity says so. CARBON DIOXIDE: the paper argues the laboratory's CO2 content contributes little more than one unit in the seventh decimal. SUPERSEDED FOR METROLOGY. Ciddor 1996 is what a modern metrology laboratory uses; this paper is used here because it is the accessible primary and because at the precision an immersion index is needed to, the two agree.
